intro: Try answering the prompts at the end of each chapter before reading these concise model backs. Return after one day, one week, and one month. Short recall repeated several times is usually more useful than one very long reread.

cards.front: Which two great river basins anchor many early Chinese agricultural histories?

015.deck: Persia and the Politics of Empire

cards.front: Conventional overall dates of the Achaemenid Empire?
cards.back: Approximately 550–330 BCE.

cards.front: Region associated with the Persian dynastic heartland?
cards.back: Parsa/Fars in southwestern Iran, linked with the Zagros and Iranian plateau.

cards.front: Who defeated Astyages of Media around 550 BCE?
cards.back: Cyrus II, later called Cyrus the Great.
539 BCE.

cards.front: Which western Anatolian kingdom did Cyrus conquer?
cards.back: Lydia, with its capital at Sardis.

cards.front: Main language of the Cyrus Cylinder?
cards.back: Akkadian, in the Babylonian dialect and cuneiform script.

cards.front: Why is the Cyrus Cylinder not a modern rights charter?
cards.back: It legitimizes kingship and cult restoration rather than universal individual civil rights.

cards.front: Which Persian ruler conquered Egypt in 525 BCE?
cards.back: Cambyses II, successor to Cyrus.

cards.front: Who came to the throne during the crisis of 522 BCE?
cards.back: Darius I.

cards.front: Which three languages are prominent at Behistun?
cards.back: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.

cards.front: Why is a “land” in an inscription not necessarily a satrapy?
cards.back: Royal lists express claims about peoples and authority, not always uniform fiscal districts.

cards.front: Name one administrative role of roads or relay stations.
cards.back: Moving royal instructions, officials, supplies or military communications across distance.
A royal dynastic center associated with Cyrus in the Persian heartland.

cards.front: What was Persepolis especially known for?
cards.back: Monumental royal ceremonial architecture and reliefs, alongside administrative archives.

cards.front: Name one language used in the Persepolis Fortification Archive.
cards.back: Elamite; some materials use Aramaic and other languages.

cards.front: What do the Persepolis tablets help historians study?
cards.back: Food allocations, travel, officials, workers and administrative economy.

cards.front: Which international administrative language was widespread in the empire?
cards.back: Aramaic.

cards.front: Which Iranian deity appears in Darius’s royal inscriptions?
cards.back: Ahuramazda.

cards.front: Why is a uniform label “Zoroastrian” for every Achaemenid practice uncertain?
cards.back: Early royal religious evidence differs from later religious traditions, and the empire was diverse.

cards.front: Year of the Ionian Revolt’s beginning?
cards.back: 499 BCE.

cards.front: Years of Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea?
cards.back: Thermopylae 480, Salamis 480, Plataea 479 BCE.

cards.front: What happened to Egypt for much of the fourth century BCE?
cards.back: It achieved effective independence from Persian rule before reconquest around 343/342 BCE.

cards.front: Who challenged Artaxerxes II in 401 BCE?
cards.back: His brother, Cyrus the Younger.

cards.front: In which year did Alexander defeat Darius III at Gaugamela?
cards.back: 331 BCE.

cards.front: What is the essential distinction between ending a dynasty and ending its institutions?
cards.back: A ruling family can fall while populations, roads, practices, cities and offices continue in altered forms.

016.deck: The Greek World and Its Political Experiments

cards.front: What does polis mean in ancient Greece?
cards.back: A civic community with town, territory, laws, institutions and citizens—not merely a walled town.

cards.front: Which script records Mycenaean palace Greek?
cards.back: Linear B.

cards.front: A key limitation of Homer for Bronze Age history?
cards.back: The poems were composed centuries later through oral and literary traditions.

cards.front: What writing system did Greeks adapt?
cards.back: A Phoenician-derived West Semitic alphabet, with consistent signs for vowels.
The first recorded Olympiad in later reckoning; not necessarily the beginning of athletic contests.

cards.front: Name one Greek overseas settlement zone.
cards.back: Sicily, southern Italy, the Black Sea, southern France or parts of North Africa.

cards.front: What did tyrannos mean in Archaic politics?
cards.back: A ruler with exceptional, irregular one-man power, not necessarily a uniquely cruel leader.

cards.front: What is selection of office by lottery called?

cards.front: Why is Africa not one historical story?
cards.back: Different regions, political institutions, ecological conditions and periods create multiple histories.

cards.front: What does 'Bantu' primarily describe in this context?

cards.front: Who was the oba of Benin?

cards.front: What was Kongo's response to Portuguese contact?

cards.front: Why must trade goods be distinguished from a producer's income?

cards.front: Why must we avoid one narrative for all preconquest America?
cards.back: Different climates, histories, communities and political institutions; no single empire governed the hemisphere.

cards.front: What is a vertical economy in the Andes?
cards.back: Access to complementary resources at different altitudes by trade, settlement or social ties.

cards.front: Where and when did Caral-Supe flourish?

cards.front: What is a hallmark of Olmec art?

cards.front: Were the Classic Maya one empire?
cards.back: No. Multiple city-states and kingdoms competed, allied and exchanged goods.

cards.front: What type of writing did the Maya use?
cards.back: A logosyllabic script with word signs and syllabic signs.

cards.front: What does the Maya Long Count record?
cards.back: Elapsed days from a conventional mythic epoch, enabling historical date notation.

cards.front: What does 'Classic Maya collapse' NOT mean?
cards.back: It does not mean Maya peoples or cultures disappeared; local dynasties and settlements changed.

cards.front: What was the Mexica-led Triple Alliance?
cards.back: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, a coalition that expanded tributary influence.
Intensively managed raised planting surfaces in shallow lake environments.

cards.front: Where did Chavín de Huántar flourish?
cards.back: At a ritual and architectural center in the highlands of modern Peru.

cards.front: What is one achievement associated with the Moche?
cards.back: Elaborate ceramics, burial practices, irrigation and large ceremonial architecture.
Large human-made geoglyphs in the desert of southern Peru.

cards.front: Name two major pre-Inka states or cultural formations.
cards.back: Examples: Wari, Tiwanaku and Chimú.
The Inka imperial realm, traditionally translated as the four regions together.
Organized rotating labor obligations for state and other collective projects.
The extensive Andean road system integrating imperial centers and many local routes.
A knotted-cord information and administrative recording device.
An ancestral Pueblo ceremonial and regional center in the U.S. Southwest.
A large Mississippian political and ceremonial settlement near present-day St. Louis.

cards.front: Why did some communities construct earthworks without large farming states?
cards.back: Coordinated gatherings and ritual projects could draw on fishing, hunting and exchange.

cards.front: What has LiDAR changed in Amazonian archaeology?
cards.back: It reveals earthworks, roads, platforms and modified landscapes beneath some forest canopies.

cards.front: Why should Indigenous alliances be included in 16th-century conquest explanations?
cards.back: Indigenous allies, political divisions, disease and long campaigns shaped the invasions.

cards.front: What is wrong with describing 1492 as the beginning of American history?
cards.back: Indigenous people already knew, inhabited and governed lands across the hemisphere for millennia.

020.deck: The Rise of Islam and the Caliphates

cards.back: The period connecting the ancient and medieval Mediterranean and western Asian worlds, with enduring and changing imperial and religious institutions.

cards.front: What are three different ways of life in pre-Islamic Arabia?
cards.back: Oasis agriculture and markets; mobile pastoralism; coastal and southern farming, ports or trade.

cards.front: What were the Byzantine and Sasanian empires?
cards.back: The eastern Roman Empire and the Iranian Sasanian Empire; both shaped the seventh-century setting.

cards.front: What is the Qur'an in Islam?
cards.back: The central sacred scripture of Islam, understood by Muslims as revelation from God to Muhammad.

cards.front: Why must sira and hadith sources be evaluated carefully?
cards.back: They were compiled and transmitted through later networks; examine genre, timing, transmission and corroboration.
Muhammad’s first wife and an important supporter in Islamic tradition.

cards.front: What was the Hijra and when did it occur?
cards.back: The migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, the starting point of the Hijri era.
The community organized around Islamic belief and collective obligations.

cards.front: Who were the muhajirun and ansar?
cards.back: The emigrants from Mecca and the supporters in Medina.

cards.front: What does the Constitution of Medina refer to?
cards.back: Early agreements describing obligations and relationships among groups in Medina; their form is debated.
In 632 CE.
A successor/deputy who leads the Muslim community or caliphal state; the office evolved.

cards.front: Who were the four Rashidun caliphs in Sunni tradition?
cards.back: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.
Abu Bakr’s campaigns to consolidate Medina’s authority after Muhammad’s death.

cards.front: What is the difference between conquest and conversion?
cards.back: One establishes political power; the other is personal or communal religious adoption.

cards.front: What were Kufa, Basra and Fustat?
cards.back: Early garrison towns that grew into important administrative, commercial and scholarly centers.

cards.front: What is the traditional Uthmanic standardization account?
cards.back: The traditional account of producing and circulating authoritative Qur’anic written exemplars under Uthman.
Civil conflict beginning in 656 over leadership, justice and political authority in the Muslim community.
Husayn ibn Ali and followers were killed; the event became a defining memory, especially for Shia Muslims.

cards.front: When and where did the Umayyad dynasty rule from its chief center?
cards.back: From 661 to 750, with Damascus a central seat of power.

cards.front: What was the Dome of the Rock?
cards.back: An Umayyad Islamic shrine in Jerusalem, completed around 691–692.

cards.front: What is the difference between Arabization and Islamization?
cards.back: Arabization is the spread of Arabic language/culture; Islamization is religious conversion/adoption.
Non-Arab clients or converts associated with Arab groups, of varied social standing.

cards.front: What changed in the Abbasid revolution of 750?
cards.back: Abbasid rule replaced the Syrian-centered Umayyads and shifted the political focus toward Iraq.

cards.front: When was Baghdad founded and by whom?
cards.back: In 762, by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur.

cards.front: What was the Abbasid translation movement?
cards.back: Translation, study and development of knowledge across Greek, Syriac, Persian, Sanskrit, Arabic and other traditions.
Human scholarly interpretation and reasoning about Islamic law and religious obligations.
A transmitted report concerning Muhammad’s words, actions or approvals.
An Abbasid-era doctrinal inquisition beginning in 833 that challenged scholars about the Qur’an’s status.

cards.front: Why does the decline of one caliphate not imply the end of Islamic civilization?
cards.back: Political centers fragmented, but Muslim communities, scholarship, worship, trade and institutions continued across regions.

021.deck: Medieval Eurasia and the Silk Roads

cards.front: What chronological focus does Chapter 21 use?
cards.back: Approximately 500–1200 CE, with earlier background and a transition toward the Mongol age.

cards.front: Why is the term “Silk Roads” plural?
cards.back: They formed multiple shifting land and maritime routes, not one uninterrupted road.

cards.front: What is a relay trade network?
cards.back: Goods pass through successive merchants or markets; each person need not travel the whole route.

cards.front: Which desert encouraged oasis routes around its edges in northwestern China?
cards.back: The Taklamakan Desert.
A roadside lodging and service station for travelers or caravans, varying by time and place.

cards.front: Which Central Asian people became famous as international merchants during much of late antiquity and the early medieval era?
cards.back: The Sogdians.
A dispersed community whose commercial and social links connect several towns or regions.

cards.front: Why are the Sogdian Ancient Letters important?
cards.back: They preserve early evidence of Sogdian commercial ties, family concerns and disrupted exchange.

cards.front: What are Dunhuang and the Mogao Library Cave?
cards.back: A major oasis town and nearby Buddhist cave complex with unusually rich surviving manuscripts.
A realm or confederation led by a khagan, found especially in Inner Asian political history.

cards.front: What was the Tang dynasty's approximate period?
What was the An Lushan rebellion?
cards.back: A major rebellion beginning in 755 that weakened Tang authority and altered frontier politics.

cards.front: How did the Tibetan Empire shape Inner Asian exchange?
cards.back: Its military and political control of parts of the highland and Tarim corridors affected movement and Buddhist networks.
A seventh-century Chinese Buddhist monk who traveled to South Asia and recorded places and religious life.

cards.front: What does the Xi'an Stele of 781 attest?
cards.back: An officially commemorated Church of the East Christian community in Tang China.

cards.front: Name two religions other than Buddhism and Islam found in historical Central Asian networks.
cards.back: Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism and Christianity are examples.

cards.front: What was the Samanid dynasty important for?
cards.back: The ninth–tenth-century Persianate and Islamic political and cultural flourishing centered partly on Bukhara.

cards.front: Why was Bukhara more than a caravan stop?
cards.back: It depended on farms, irrigation, workshops, learning and regional markets as well as caravans.
A major Buddhist monastic and scholastic center in what is now Bihar, India.

cards.front: Which South Asian dynasty raided Srivijaya-linked centers in 1025?
cards.back: The Chola dynasty under Rajendra I.
A maritime Southeast Asian political and commercial network influential from roughly the seventh century.

cards.front: What is a monsoon in the context of Indian Ocean navigation?
cards.back: A seasonal wind system whose recurring shifts helped sailors plan Indian Ocean routes.

cards.front: Why is the Belitung shipwreck significant?
cards.back: An important ninth-century wreck with Chinese ceramics documenting maritime exchange.

cards.front: Give one major technological or commercial development under the Song.
cards.back: Expanded commercial cities, canals, ceramics, printing or technical experimentation.

cards.front: What was the Grand Canal's core function?
cards.back: To connect northern and southern regions of China for transport and state administration.

cards.front: Why must the Battle of Talas paper story be treated cautiously?
cards.back: The story of captured Chinese paper makers is too narrow and its evidence disputed; diffusion involved multiple processes.

cards.front: Name one river system connecting northern Europe with the Black Sea world.
cards.back: The Dnieper or Volga, among others.

cards.front: What is the difference between an object traveling and a person making the whole journey?
cards.back: Cargo can pass through multiple intermediaries; the original maker may never see the destination.
A route or connection whose disruption affects access, cost or traffic through a larger network.

cards.front: How will Chapter 22 change the Silk Roads story?
cards.back: It reorganized preexisting networks through conquest and new political conditions, with severe violence and increased travel in some periods.

022.deck: The Mongols and the Connected World

cards.front: What does pastoralism mean in the steppe context?
cards.back: An animal-herding livelihood based partly on seasonal pasture movement.

cards.front: Who was Temüjin, and what title did he receive in 1206?
cards.back: Temujin became Chinggis Khan at the 1206 assembly.
A political assembly of steppe elites, including important selections of rulers.

cards.front: Name two features of Mongol military organization beyond mounted archery.
cards.back: Scouting, coordinated commands, decimal units, siege engineers or royal guards.

cards.front: Why is forage central to evaluating medieval army-size claims?
cards.back: Large numbers of horses required food, water, grazing and feasible routes.

cards.front: Which two northern Chinese or northwestern states were major early Mongol opponents?
cards.back: Western Xia (Tangut) and Jin (Jurchen).

cards.front: In which year did Chinggis Khan die?
Which empire was attacked after the Otrar crisis?
cards.back: The Khwarazmian Empire.

cards.front: Why are exact casualty figures in medieval conquest accounts difficult to trust?
cards.back: Writers could exaggerate, copy figures or lack accurate population information.

cards.front: Name the four principal branches traditionally linked to Chinggis Khan's sons.
cards.back: Jochi, Chagatai, Ogedei and Tolui.

cards.front: Who succeeded Chinggis Khan as great khan in 1229?
cards.back: Ogedei Khan.

cards.front: Name one influential woman in Mongol succession politics.
cards.back: Toregene Khatun or Sorghaghtani Beki, among others.

cards.front: In which year did Kyiv fall to Mongol forces?
What was the Jochid ulus commonly called in later history?
cards.back: The Golden Horde.

cards.front: What did Mongol khans often require from Rus' rulers?
cards.back: Tribute and recognition of khanly authority; arrangements varied.

cards.front: Which city fell to Hülegü's forces in 1258?
cards.back: Baghdad.

cards.front: Who defeated Mongol forces at Ayn Jalut in 1260?
cards.back: The Mamluks of Egypt.

cards.front: Which Mongol ruler founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271?
cards.back: Kublai Khan.

cards.front: When was the Southern Song conquest completed?
Name the four main later Mongol-linked political realms.
cards.back: Yuan, Chagatai, Ilkhanate and Jochid/Golden Horde.

cards.front: What was the yam or jam relay network?
cards.back: A network of relay stations supplying authorized messengers.
A tablet or credential linked to official authorization and certain privileges.

cards.front: What does Pax Mongolica refer to, and why must it be qualified?
cards.back: A label for relative trade security under some Mongol regimes; it was uneven and coercive.
An imperial-era investment or commercial partnership associated with merchants.

cards.front: What is the Secret History of the Mongols?
cards.back: A thirteenth-century dynastic narrative of Mongol origins and Chinggis Khan.
A major Ilkhanid historian and court official who composed a universal history.

cards.front: What did the Issyk-Kul research identify for 1338–39?
cards.back: Plague evidence in 1338–39 burials and important ancestral genomic connections.

cards.front: Why is the Caffa catapulted-corpses account disputed?
cards.back: Its famous account is non-eyewitness and its proposed causal route is challenged.

cards.front: In what year did Yuan rule end in China?
What is the difference between connectivity and peace?
cards.back: People and goods may move widely even while warfare, exploitation and unequal security persist.
